question: What happens to oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in the body during asphyxia?

options.A: High nitrogen and low carbon dioxide
options.C: High oxygen and low carbon dioxide
options.D: Low oxygen and high carbon dioxide

explanation: Think of asphyxia as a double hit: oxygen drops while carbon dioxide builds up rapidly in the blood because the body cannot get rid of it. You've got this! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why is the brain hit the hardest when someone experiences asphyxia?

options.A: It has a high metabolic rate and constant oxygen demand
options.B: It produces its own oxygen through cellular division
options.C: It stores large reserves of backup oxygen
options.D: It is protected by cerebrospinal fluid that blocks toxins

explanation: The brain is a busy organ that constantly demands oxygen. When that supply cuts off, brain cells start struggling almost immediately. Great job reviewing this! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h1)

question: How does a person usually breathe right at the start of an asphyxia event?
explanation: At first, the body's control center panics and tries to pull in as much air as possible, resulting in fast, deep breaths to fight off the lack of oxygen. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h2)

question: What causes a patient to start having convulsions as asphyxia gets worse?

options.A: Sudden infection spreading to the spinal cord
options.B: Severe lack of oxygen affecting brain function
options.C: A massive release of digestive enzymes
options.D: Rapid cooling of the skin surface

explanation: When brain cells are starved of oxygen for too long, they start misfiring wildly. This erratic electrical activity leads to muscle twitching and convulsions. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h2)

question: Which of these is a common situation that can lead to asphyxia?

options.C: Sudden loss of blood from a wound

explanation: Being trapped in a tiny, unventilated box or room quickly uses up all the oxygen, leading to suffocation. Always keep safety in mind! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h3)

question: Why does a person trapped in a smoke-filled room suffer from asphyxia?

options.A: Severe dehydration and low blood volume
options.B: Toxic gas inhalation replacing ambient oxygen
options.D: Sudden paralysis of the heart muscle

explanation: Thick smoke and poisonous gases take up all the space in the air, pushing out the good oxygen your lungs need to function. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h3)

question: What is the medical name for the bluish color you see on a patient's skin when they lack oxygen?
explanation: Cyanosis comes from 'cyano' (blue). It happens when red blood cells lacking oxygen circulate near the skin surface. A classic clinical sign to remember! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h4)

question: Why do patients in the early stages of asphyxia often look restless and confused?

options.A: Their digestive system has shut down
options.B: The brain is not receiving enough oxygen
options.C: Their blood pressure is abnormally high
options.D: They are having an allergic skin reaction

explanation: The brain is very sensitive to oxygen levels. When it starts running low, the patient often gets anxious, confused, or restless before losing consciousness. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h4)

question: As a nurse or rescuer, what is the very first thing you must check at an emergency scene?

options.A: Ensure the safety of the surrounding environment

explanation: Safety first! Always check for dangers (like live wires or smoke) so you don't become a second victim needing rescue. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h5)

question: Why should you avoid sticking your fingers blindly into a choking patient's mouth to clear an airway?

options.A: They interfere with heart rhythm monitors
options.B: They always cause permanent bleeding of the gums
options.C: They can push the object further down the throat
options.D: They make the patient vomit large amounts of blood

explanation: Blind finger sweeps are dangerous because you might accidentally jam a loose object deeper into the windpipe. Only clear what you can actually see! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h5)

question: Which airway maneuver should you use if you think your patient has a neck or spine injury?
explanation: The jaw-thrust opens the airway without bending or moving the neck, keeping the cervical spine safe from further harm. Brilliant nursing judgment! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h6)

question: What is the main goal of passing an endotracheal tube during resuscitation?

options.A: To secure a direct passage for oxygen into the lungs
options.B: To remove fluid directly from the stomach
options.C: To prevent the patient from speaking to staff
options.D: To measure the exact weight of the patient

explanation: An endotracheal tube creates a safe, clear highway straight into the lungs, bypassing any blockages in the upper airway. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h6)

question: What is a top priority in nursing care right after a patient is revived from asphyxia?

options.A: Discharging the patient home within one hour
options.B: Continuous monitoring of breathing and oxygen levels
options.C: Encouraging the patient to eat a large meal

explanation: Just because a patient is revived doesn't mean they are out of the woods. Close watch on their vitals helps catch any sudden crashes early. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h7)

question: Why are frequent neurological checks so important after an asphyxial episode?

options.A: To detect brain injury caused by lack of oxygen
options.B: To test the function of the cranial nerves in the stomach
options.C: To check if the patient remembers their home address
options.D: To see if the patient is ready to walk unassisted

explanation: When the brain goes without oxygen, brain cells can be injured. Doing regular mental checks helps us track how well the patient is recovering. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h7)

question: Which practice helps prevent suffocation in sleeping infants?

options.A: Placing babies on their backs on a firm mattress
options.C: Dressing infants in airtight plastic wrappers
options.D: Using soft pillows and thick quilts in the cot

explanation: Back-sleeping on a firm, clutter-free baby bed is the safest way to prevent accidental suffocation in infants. You're mastering pediatric safety! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h8)

question: Why is teaching workers about toxic gases important in factories and industrial sites?

options.A: It helps workers recognize hidden breathing hazards and use safety gear
options.B: It eliminates the need for any medical staff on site
options.C: It reduces the cost of electricity in factories
options.D: It guarantees that machinery will never break down

explanation: Many toxic gases are invisible. Educating workers helps them spot dangers early and protect themselves with proper ventilation and masks. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h8)
